A self-hosted Next.js app using the built-in Node server is on an affected version. Reverse proxy logs show rare upgrade-style requests to paths that are not WebSocket routes. Two seconds later the same pod connects to the cloud metadata address and then its workload role lists storage buckets. The WAF allowed one request and blocked three later attempts. How should the SOC classify this timeline and what should happen first?

<reasoning>The decisive observation is not the upgrade header by itself; many applications use WebSockets legitimately. Here the target paths are not documented WebSocket routes, the deployment is self-hosted with the vulnerable server mode, and the pod reaches metadata within seconds of the allowed request. A benign metadata call would need a known SDK, agent, startup event, or recurring baseline, and a benign storage listing would need an application workflow or change window; none are present. The blocked attempts prove scanning continued, but the allowed request plus metadata and cloud API sequence shows a server-originated pivot rather than mere internet noise. The best hypothesis is framework SSRF followed by credential exposure and cloud discovery, so patching alone is not sufficient. The first response must preserve evidence, contain egress, and rotate or invalidate the exposed workload credentials.</reasoning>
<answer>{"summary":"Classify the allowed timeline as confirmed follow-on abuse from likely framework SSRF, while labeling the blocked attempts as attempted exploitation or scanning.","evidence":["Self-hosted Next.js built-in Node server","Affected framework version","Rare upgrade-style request to non-WebSocket paths","Allowed request followed within seconds by metadata egress","Workload role listed storage buckets after metadata access"],"missing_benign_evidence":["No legitimate WebSocket route","No SDK or agent baseline for metadata access","No change window","No application feature requiring storage enumeration"],"hypotheses":["Normal WebSocket traffic","Internet scan only","Framework SSRF with metadata access","Unrelated cloud automation"],"eliminations":["Normal WebSocket traffic fails because the paths are not WebSocket routes","Scan only fails because sensitive server egress and cloud API use followed","Unrelated automation lacks workflow and timing evidence"],"most_likely_activity":"Exploitation of a public-facing framework SSRF path leading to cloud credential exposure and cloud discovery.","mitre_techniques":["T1190","T1552.005","T1580"],"hunts":["Find other self-hosted Next.js origins with built-in server exposure and affected versions","Join suspicious upgrade request timestamps to app egress toward link-local, RFC1918, loopback, or cluster-local targets","Review every cloud API call by the affected workload identity after the first metadata request"],"actions":["Preserve WAF, proxy, app, pod, egress, and cloud audit logs","Patch or redeploy to a fixed framework version","Block unneeded upgrade traffic and direct origin reachability while patching","Restrict workload egress to approved destinations","Rotate or invalidate the workload credentials and scope cloud impact"],"confidence":"high","source_id":"concept-nextjs-ssrf-websocket-upgrade","source_book":"web_framework_security"}</answer>

An older self-hosted Next.js admin portal uses Server Actions. During a support ticket, proxy logs show unusual host and origin combinations, then the app server makes an HTTP request to an internal-only admin endpoint and returns a large response to the client path. There is no legitimate feature that fetches that endpoint. Is this CSRF, SSRF, or something else?

<reasoning>The requester that reaches the internal admin endpoint is the application server, not the user's browser. That distinction moves the case away from CSRF and into SSRF, because the attacker is abusing the server's network position and trust. The unusual host and origin pairing is a clue that request metadata influenced server-side routing or redirect behavior. A benign support workflow would require a documented internal fetch path, a matching user action, and expected response sizes; those are absent. Because there is no process execution or file write, RCE is not proven from these facts. The coherent classification is Server Actions SSRF with possible internal data exposure, requiring endpoint access review and credential scoping rather than browser-session-only response.</reasoning>
<answer>{"summary":"This is best classified as SSRF, not CSRF or proven RCE, because the server made the internal request after attacker-influenced request metadata.","evidence":["Self-hosted Next.js Server Actions","Unusual host and origin combinations","Server request to internal-only admin endpoint","Large response returned to client path","No legitimate feature for that internal endpoint"],"missing_benign_evidence":["No documented internal fetch workflow","No expected admin endpoint access by the portal","No maintenance ticket matching the request","No execution evidence proving RCE"],"hypotheses":["CSRF against a user's browser","Server-side request forgery","Remote code execution","Legitimate support workflow"],"eliminations":["CSRF is weaker because the server, not the browser, reached the internal endpoint","RCE is unproven without command, process, or file evidence","Legitimate support lacks route and ticket evidence"],"most_likely_activity":"Server-side request forgery through framework request handling that exposed an internal admin resource.","mitre_techniques":["T1190","T1552.005"],"hunts":["Search proxy logs for rare host/origin mismatches against Server Actions paths","Join those requests to server egress toward internal-only HTTP services","Review internal admin endpoint logs for response sizes and accessed objects"],"actions":["Patch the framework","Preserve proxy and application logs","Review whether secrets or admin data were returned","Restrict server egress to internal admin networks","Add host/origin validation tests for Server Actions"],"confidence":"medium-high","source_id":"concept-nextjs-server-actions-ssrf","source_book":"web_framework_security"}</answer>

A patched web gateway blocks most cross-origin requests, but logs show state-changing Server Action posts where the origin value is null and the user's valid cookies are present. There is no server egress to metadata or internal admin hosts. The business owner asks whether this is the same as the Next.js SSRF issue. How should VIRGIL explain the distinction?

<reasoning>The key detail is whose trust context is being abused. In this timeline the browser carries the user's cookies and submits a state-changing action with an opaque or null origin, while the server does not make a suspicious outbound request to internal resources. That points to CSRF-style browser session abuse, not SSRF. A true SSRF case would require server-originated egress to metadata, loopback, private ranges, cluster-local services, or internal APIs. A benign explanation would need a same-site form, valid CSRF token, and expected origin validation path; those are not established. The answer should separate containment: revoke or protect user sessions and patch origin validation for CSRF, while reserving credential rotation for cases with metadata or secret exposure.</reasoning>
<answer>{"summary":"Treat this as CSRF-style Server Action abuse, not SSRF, because the browser supplied the authenticated request and no server-side internal egress appears.","evidence":["State-changing Server Action posts","Origin value is null","Valid user cookies present","No metadata egress","No internal admin egress"],"missing_benign_evidence":["No valid CSRF token evidence","No expected same-site origin","No documented sandboxed workflow","No server-side egress indicators"],"hypotheses":["Server-side request forgery","Cross-site request forgery","Normal same-site form submission","Remote code execution"],"eliminations":["SSRF lacks server-originated internal egress","RCE lacks execution telemetry","Normal form submission lacks origin and token evidence"],"most_likely_activity":"CSRF-style abuse of Server Actions where browser session context performs unauthorized state changes.","mitre_techniques":["T1189"],"hunts":["Find state-changing Server Action requests with null, missing, or unexpected origins","Correlate actions to user reports and browser sessions","Review sensitive object changes made during the window"],"actions":["Patch the affected framework version","Require robust CSRF controls for sensitive actions","Invalidate impacted user sessions if changes occurred","Review state changes rather than cloud metadata access as the primary impact path"],"confidence":"medium-high","source_id":"concept-nextjs-server-actions-csrf-origin-null","source_book":"web_framework_security"}</answer>

Cloud engineering says they cannot patch all self-hosted framework apps today. You can deploy temporary network controls. Which egress restrictions reduce SSRF impact without relying on exact exploit signatures?

<reasoning>SSRF succeeds because the server can reach resources the attacker cannot reach directly. Signature blocking at ingress helps, but it is brittle when the framework bug can be reached through many request shapes. The durable control is to remove unnecessary destinations from the app server's egress path. A benign application egress profile should have known APIs, package mirrors, telemetry collectors, and backend services; it should not need open access to metadata, loopback admin listeners, broad RFC1918 space, or cluster control planes. If an app legitimately needs metadata, it should use scoped identity mechanisms and explicit exceptions, not unrestricted link-local access. The temporary policy should therefore deny sensitive network classes by default, allow only business destinations, and log denials as detection leads.</reasoning>
<answer>{"summary":"Use default-deny egress for app workloads, explicitly allow required business destinations, and block metadata, loopback, broad private ranges, cluster-local control planes, and internal admin services unless approved.","evidence":["Patching cannot finish today","Self-hosted framework apps are potentially exposed","SSRF impact depends on server reachability","Exact exploit signatures are fragile"],"missing_benign_evidence":["No documented need for broad RFC1918 egress","No approved metadata access requirement for every app","No reason public web frontends should reach internal admin planes"],"hypotheses":["Ingress signatures are enough","Patch delay can be offset by egress reduction","Metadata access must remain open for all workloads","Only vulnerable paths matter"],"eliminations":["Ingress-only signatures miss variant request shapes","Universal metadata access is unnecessary and high impact","Vulnerability path matters less if the server cannot reach valuable targets"],"most_likely_activity":"Risk-reduction control for possible SSRF exploitation by constraining server-originated requests.","mitre_techniques":["T1190","T1552.005"],"hunts":["Alert on denied egress from web workloads to metadata, loopback, cluster-local, and internal admin ranges","Baseline normal app egress before and after policy","Review workloads with policy exceptions for excessive identity privileges"],"actions":["Deny link-local metadata access except through approved identity paths","Deny loopback and broad RFC1918 egress from public web workloads","Allow explicit backend/API destinations only","Log and alert on denials during patch rollout","Prioritize patching apps that require sensitive exceptions"],"confidence":"high","source_id":"concept-framework-ssrf-egress-policy","source_book":"web_framework_security"}</answer>

In a training lab, app-a is patched and has a normal chat WebSocket route. App-b is vulnerable and receives a blocked upgrade-style request with no follow-on egress. App-c is vulnerable and receives an allowed upgrade-style request followed by metadata access and a secrets-manager list call. How should learners classify these three timelines?

<reasoning>The classification must use the full sequence rather than one indicator. App-a has the strongest benign explanation: patched version, documented WebSocket route, and normal behavior. App-b has exposure and suspicious inbound traffic, but the block decision and absence of follow-on egress keep it at attempted exploitation rather than compromise. App-c has every escalation signal: vulnerable deployment, allowed suspicious request, server egress to metadata, and cloud API activity that implies credential use. A benign story for app-c would require a documented metadata workflow and secrets enumeration baseline, which are absent from the lab facts. The correct lesson is that inbound anomalies start the hunt, but egress and control-plane follow-on determine severity.</reasoning>
<answer>{"summary":"Classify app-a as benign or low priority, app-b as attempted SSRF or scan, and app-c as confirmed follow-on abuse.","evidence":["App-a is patched and has a normal chat WebSocket route","App-b is vulnerable but the request was blocked and no egress followed","App-c is vulnerable and had allowed suspicious inbound traffic","App-c reached metadata","App-c performed secrets-manager listing"],"missing_benign_evidence":["No app-c metadata workflow","No app-c secrets-manager baseline","No app-b egress impact","No app-a anomalous route"],"hypotheses":["Every upgrade request is malicious","Blocked request equals compromise","Metadata plus secrets access indicates credential impact","Patched WebSocket apps are always suspicious"],"eliminations":["Legitimate WebSocket routes exist","Blocked inbound without impact is not compromise by itself","Cloud control-plane follow-on after metadata access is high-severity impact evidence"],"most_likely_activity":"Mixed lab outcomes: benign WebSocket behavior, attempted exploitation, and successful SSRF with credential abuse.","mitre_techniques":["T1190","T1552.005"],"hunts":["Join ingress anomalies to egress and cloud audit by app identity","Track WAF allowed versus blocked disposition","Separate patched legitimate WebSocket routes from unexpected upgrade paths"],"actions":["Document app-a as control case","Monitor app-b and verify patching","Contain app-c, rotate credentials, and scope secrets access","Use these labels to train analysts away from single-indicator conclusions"],"confidence":"high","source_id":"concept-framework-ssrf-lab-classification","source_book":"web_framework_security"}</answer>

Threat intel mentions a React Server Components issue and a Next.js SSRF issue in the same weekly briefing. On one host, the app process writes a new script, spawns a shell, and opens an outbound session. There is no metadata request. Should the incident lead handle this like SSRF?

<reasoning>The observed artifacts point to execution, not request forgery. A framework SSRF case is centered on server-originated HTTP access to internal or metadata resources after a suspicious inbound request; it may have no new process at all. Here the app process writes a script, spawns a shell, and establishes outbound communication, which fits code execution and post-exploitation behavior. A benign deployment would have a release record, package manager activity, and signed or expected scripts; those are not described. The absence of metadata traffic does not make the incident benign, it changes the response lane. The lead should treat this as app-server compromise with host forensics, persistence review, and credential scoping, while not overfitting the investigation to SSRF indicators.</reasoning>
<answer>{"summary":"Handle this as likely framework-related RCE or app-server compromise, not as SSRF, because process execution and file creation are the primary evidence.","evidence":["App process wrote a new script","App process spawned a shell","Outbound session opened","No metadata request observed"],"missing_benign_evidence":["No deployment record","No package manager event","No signed expected script","No known admin session"],"hypotheses":["SSRF","Remote code execution","Legitimate deployment","Monitoring agent behavior"],"eliminations":["SSRF is unsupported without server-side internal or metadata egress","Legitimate deployment lacks release evidence","Monitoring agents should not be spawned by the app process through a shell"],"most_likely_activity":"Remote code execution or app-server compromise through a framework boundary issue.","mitre_techniques":["T1190","T1059","T1105"],"hunts":["Search for app-worker child shells across hosts","Review script file creation paths, hashes, and owners","Correlate inbound requests to first process execution","Check persistence, credential access, and outbound destinations"],"actions":["Contain the host or workload","Preserve disk, memory, app logs, and process telemetry","Patch the relevant framework or dependency","Rotate secrets available to the app process","Do not limit the scope to metadata access"],"confidence":"medium-high","source_id":"concept-framework-rsc-rce-not-ssrf","source_book":"web_framework_security"}</answer>

A containerized web app made one metadata request immediately after suspicious inbound framework traffic. Cloud audit then shows GetCallerIdentity, ListSecrets, and one failed CreateAccessKey attempt by the same role. The app team says the container was patched twenty minutes later. Is patching enough?

<reasoning>Patching removes the vulnerable request primitive going forward, but it does not undo credentials that may already have been exposed. The metadata request immediately after suspicious inbound traffic is the first impact clue, and the subsequent identity check, secrets listing, and access-key attempt show the role was used beyond normal application behavior. A benign cloud SDK flow would not normally list secrets or attempt key creation unless the app is designed for identity administration, which is not stated. The failed CreateAccessKey attempt is especially important because it suggests the actor tested persistence or credential materialization. The correct response is credential containment and cloud scoping in addition to patching. Treat the role as exposed until logs prove otherwise.</reasoning>
<answer>{"summary":"Patching is necessary but insufficient; metadata access plus follow-on cloud API behavior requires credential rotation, permission review, and full scope of role activity.","evidence":["Metadata request followed suspicious inbound framework traffic","Same role called GetCallerIdentity","Same role listed secrets","Failed CreateAccessKey attempt","Patch happened after the suspicious activity"],"missing_benign_evidence":["No normal secret-listing workflow","No identity-administration feature","No approved cloud maintenance","No evidence credentials were invalidated before use"],"hypotheses":["Patch fully resolves the case","Normal cloud SDK behavior","Credential exposure through SSRF","False positive metadata access"],"eliminations":["Patch does not revoke already exposed credentials","Normal SDK behavior does not explain secrets listing and key creation attempt","False positive is weakened by control-plane follow-on"],"most_likely_activity":"SSRF-mediated cloud credential exposure followed by cloud discovery and attempted credential persistence.","mitre_techniques":["T1190","T1552.005","T1580","T1098"],"hunts":["Enumerate all cloud API calls by the role from first metadata access onward","Search for secrets reads, role assumptions, key creation attempts, and storage listing","Identify other workloads with the same role or equivalent policy"],"actions":["Rotate or invalidate role sessions and any secrets accessed","Constrain role permissions and egress","Patch or redeploy the app","Preserve cloud audit and network logs","Report residual risk until credential-use scope is complete"],"confidence":"high","source_id":"concept-ssrf-cloud-credential-response","source_book":"web_framework_security"}</answer>

Asset inventory finds 70 Next.js services after an SSRF advisory. Ten are managed-hosted, twenty are static exports, fifteen are self-hosted but patched, and twenty-five are self-hosted with affected versions. Of the affected group, five have metadata egress and two have follow-on cloud API calls. How should the patch and IR queues be ordered?

<reasoning>The queue must separate vulnerability exposure from compromise evidence. Managed-hosted and static exports may still need verification, but they do not match the high-risk self-hosted built-in server exposure described by the advisory. Patched self-hosted systems need monitoring and configuration checks, not the first emergency slot unless they show impact. The twenty-five self-hosted affected services are the patch priority, but the five with metadata egress outrank the rest for investigation. The two with cloud API follow-on outrank even the other metadata cases because they show possible credential use after exposure. A purely version-based queue would waste time on lower-impact cases while confirmed-impact services continue to use potentially exposed credentials.</reasoning>
